r: Introduction to Music asks non-majors to build a vocabulary for describing structure, style, genre, and aesthetic meaning across diverse musical traditions, then apply that vocabulary through guided listening. Large language models already generate competent program notes, genre comparisons, and stylistic analyses from text prompts, and observed-usage data shows writing and descriptive-explanation tasks are heavily used in consumer AI activity today. What AI cannot yet reliably replace is the live, iterative listening practice the Honors seminar format emphasizes, where instructors probe interpretation through discussion and immediate follow-up questions. Multimodal audio analysis remains uneven for nuanced timbral or stylistic judgments in 2026, so instrumental need is only partially reduced. The GT-Pathways designation binds this course into the statutory transfer core regardless of automatability, which keeps near-term substitution symbolic rather than practical for degree planning purposes today.

By 2031, multimodal models should describe recorded music, compare genres, and draft aesthetic-interpretation essays with greater reliability, and task-exposure research already classifies writing-adjacent descriptive work as strongly positively associated with AI exposure. Productivity studies on professional writing show large time savings with quality gains, a pattern plausibly transferable to music-appreciation coursework such as program notes or listening journals. Still, the Honors seminar's interactive-discussion format, where students defend interpretations aloud and adjust to peer challenge, resists full digitization even as underlying content generation improves. Diffusion data suggests campus adoption of AI listening tools will lag raw capability, tempering how quickly this shifts. The GT-AH1 designation continues capping instrumental displacement at a moderate level, since the course remains embedded in a statutory gen-ed requirement independent of how well AI performs the descriptive tasks themselves.

A ten-year horizon is genuinely uncertain for arts-appreciation coursework: capability trends point toward continued doubling of AI task-time horizons, which would plausibly let systems handle sophisticated cross-genre aesthetic commentary and personalized listening guidance competently. If diffusion catches up with capability, the descriptive and interpretive work this course teaches could be substantially reproducible by AI companions embedded in music platforms. Yet the Honors seminar's live discussion component and the GT-Pathways transfer-core mandate both persist as structural anchors independent of AI competence, so this is not a confident prediction of displacement. Aesthetic interpretation also carries low error cost, meaning verification burden will not be the limiting factor by then; institutional and pedagogical inertia, not technical capability, is the more binding constraint on how far instrumental need actually erodes.
HON 1000.d: In this course, students investigate the function, structure, style and genre classifications, and aesthetic interpretations of a diverse variety of musical traditions. The students develop and employ a vocabulary for musical description and listen to many different traditions of musical expression. This course is intended for non-music majors.

r: Introduction to Chicana/o Studies asks students to synthesize interdisciplinary material spanning history, sociology, political science, anthropology, and art history into coherent analysis of Mexican-origin cultural and political experience, then discuss contested interpretations of colonialism and identity in seminar. Current models can draft historical summaries and cross-disciplinary syntheses competently, aligning with observed-usage data showing writing and research-adjacent tasks dominate consumer AI activity today. However, the course's core work is contested, identity-adjacent interpretation where getting nuance wrong carries real reputational and pedagogical cost, and the jagged-frontier findings show AI users trust outputs poorly calibrated to actual accuracy outside a model's strong suit. That verification burden, paired with the Honors seminar's discussion-heavy format, keeps a human instructor's judgment central to evaluating student interpretation, so instrumental need remains largely intact at this horizon.

By 2031, AI drafting of historical and cultural background will likely be routine, and task-exposure research continues to associate synthesis-heavy writing work with high exposure, suggesting students and instructors alike will lean on AI for source gathering and first-draft synthesis. But the discipline's central skill, adjudicating contested claims about power, colonialism, and cultural representation, remains adversarial in the sense that getting it wrong is not obviously self-correcting, so verification burden stays elevated even as raw content generation improves. Enterprise adoption data suggests professional and educational use of AI for interpretive writing will keep growing, but unevenly. The GT-SS3 designation continues to anchor the course in the statutory gen-ed core, which caps how far even substantial capability gains can translate into reduced instrumental need for the course itself.

Ten years out, capability trends imply AI could handle much of the historical and cultural synthesis this course currently teaches, and if verification tools mature enough to catch subtle interpretive bias, the low-verification-burden ceiling that protects the course today could erode. That is a real possibility, not a confident forecast: identity-related interpretation is exactly the kind of contested, non-obvious-failure domain where jagged-frontier research suggests AI users remain poorly calibrated even as raw competence rises. Institutional lock-in through the GT-Pathways transfer core persists independent of capability, and the Honors seminar's discussion format is unlikely to disappear even if content generation is largely automated. On balance, moderate rather than extensive erosion of instrumental need seems most defensible, contingent on both verification-tooling progress and how discussion-based pedagogy adapts.
HON 1003.d: This course introduces students to the broad range of the interdisciplinary field of Chicana/o Studies. The course covers the major historical moments beginning with an overview of Pre- Columbian civilizations in the Americas and Medieval Spain, which have led to the contemporary social location of Mexican-origin population within the United States. In addition, the course introduces students to the broad scope of Chicana/o cultural production in the creative arts such as visual, film, music and literature. Resources draw from various disciplines, including but not limited to: sociology, history, political science, anthropology, education, art and art history, women and gender studies, and religious studies.

r: The Big Questions introduces philosophical inquiry into knowledge, reality, and existence, explicitly training students not in facts but in how to reason rigorously and open-endedly about contested claims, mirrored in live Socratic-style Honors seminar discussion. This is precisely the profile task-exposure research flags as protected: critical-reasoning and science-adjacent skills are strongly negatively associated with AI exposure, unlike writing or programming tasks. Current models can summarize philosophical positions but cannot reliably substitute for the iterative, adversarial questioning that builds a student's own reasoning capacity, and the jagged-frontier evidence shows AI users overtrust outputs on exactly this kind of open-ended, non-obvious-failure task. Verification burden here is maximal because the entire point is developing the human's own judgment, not producing a deliverable, so instrumental need for the course remains essentially undiminished at this horizon.

By 2031, AI will likely produce fluent summaries of philosophical arguments and even generate plausible-sounding counterarguments, and capability-trend research points to continued fast improvement in extended reasoning tasks. Even so, the course's actual output is a trained human reasoner, not a document, and task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking skills are negatively associated with exposure should persist because the skill being taught is not one AI performs on the student's behalf in any meaningful sense. Productivity gains documented elsewhere for professional writing do not transfer cleanly to a pedagogy built on live, adversarial dialogue. Some erosion is plausible if students substitute AI-assisted essay drafting for genuine engagement, but that reflects misuse rather than the course's tasks becoming AI-competent, so the verification-burden protection should largely hold.

A ten-year view carries real uncertainty about how thoroughly AI reasoning assistants get woven into Socratic pedagogy itself, potentially as sparring partners rather than replacements, and METR-style capability-horizon trends suggest systems capable of sustained, coherent multi-step argumentation are plausible by then. But the deterministic core of this course, that students must build their own capacity for rigorous open-ended reasoning under real-time challenge, does not become instrumentally unnecessary merely because AI can also produce arguments; the skill and the deliverable are different things here. Task-exposure research's negative association between critical-thinking demand and exposure is the most durable protective factor identified across the evidence base, and nothing in current trends suggests it inverts. Confidence in continued low displacement remains warranted, though not absolute.
HON 1011.d: Philosophy asks questions such as: What am I? How can I know things? What is real? Does God exist? Students confront questions like these in a rigorous, critical, and open-ended manner. Philosophy is unlike other disciplines: students learn not just what others have discovered, but also how to think about themselves, the world, and the relation between them.

r: Presentational Speaking teaches students to organize, draft, and deliver ethical presentations across professional and public contexts, emphasizing audience adaptation, technology use, and live delivery skill alongside listening and critical-thinking components. AI already drafts and refines speech content and slide outlines well, consistent with observed-usage data showing writing tasks dominate consumer AI activity, so the planning half of this course's work is meaningfully AI-assisted today. But the graded, instrumental core is live performance: vocal delivery, nonverbal presence, real-time audience reading, and adaptation under pressure, which are embodied, in-person skills no text or voice model performs for the student. This split keeps instrumental need substantial: content generation is exposed, but the actual competency being certified, delivering effectively in person, is not something AI can do on a student's behalf.

By 2031, AI presentation-coaching tools should give increasingly sophisticated feedback on pacing, filler words, and structure, and productivity research on similar coaching-style interventions shows meaningful gains especially for less experienced performers, suggesting real augmentation value for students practicing delivery. Content drafting will likely be almost fully AI-assisted by this point. Still, the embodied act of standing before an audience, reading its reactions, and adjusting delivery in real time remains outside what any deployed AI system performs instead of the student; task-exposure research consistently treats interpersonal, real-time performance as low-exposure relative to writing tasks. The oral-communication general-studies requirement anchors the course in degree structure independent of these dynamics. Moderate rather than extensive displacement of instrumental need looks most defensible at this horizon.

Ten years out, AI avatars or coaching agents capable of near-real-time delivery feedback are plausible given the pace of capability improvement documented in task-horizon research, and such tools could meaningfully compress how much practice time students need outside class. Whether that constitutes eliminating instrumental need for the course itself is a different question: live, in-person presentation before a human audience is the credentialed skill, and embodiment protections identified across the evidence base do not weaken merely because rehearsal tools improve. Content-generation tasks within the course likely approach near-full automation by then. Genuine uncertainty remains about how thoroughly interpersonal performance skill itself gets reframed by ubiquitous AI coaching, but a confident prediction of substantial course-level displacement is not warranted by current evidence.
HON 1013.d: This course teaches students how to design and deliver effective, ethical presentations. The ability to adapt to different audiences and contexts - such as professional or public situations - is emphasized. The course provides instruction on and practice of organization, delivery and performance, technology, and research skills. Students also learn effective listening techniques and critical thinking skills. The course empowers students to become successful professional presenters and public speakers.

r: Comparative Politics has students examine and contrast political structures, ideologies, and institutional issues across modern states, work that is substantially analytical and text-based rather than performative. Current models handle comparative institutional description and structured argument drafting well, and observed-usage data confirms writing and analytical tasks are prominent in both consumer and enterprise AI activity today. The Honors seminar format layers in live discussion and debate over contested political interpretations, which introduces a verification and calibration concern: jagged-frontier research shows AI users are less accurate and poorly calibrated once discussion moves outside a model's confident zone, such as normatively contested comparisons. That keeps meaningful instrumental need intact even though background content generation is already exposed, since the course's graded value lies partly in live analytical discussion, not just descriptive output.

By 2031, AI-assisted comparative analysis of political systems should be routine and increasingly reliable for descriptive and structural comparison, consistent with capability-trend research showing steady improvement on extended analytical tasks. Enterprise-style automation patterns, where AI increasingly completes rather than merely assists tasks, suggest students could offload substantial first-draft comparative writing. The seminar's discussion component, requiring students to defend interpretive claims about contested political systems in real time, should continue resisting full substitution, though the margin narrows as reasoning models improve. The GT-SS1 designation keeps the course tied to the statutory transfer core regardless of these capability shifts. On balance, moderate instrumental displacement is defensible, driven by content-generation exposure rather than by the interpretive-discussion core of the course actually being automated away.

A ten-year outlook for comparative political analysis is genuinely uncertain: if reasoning-model capability keeps compounding at rates implied by task-horizon-doubling research, AI could plausibly produce sophisticated, well-calibrated comparative political analysis rivaling much of what this course teaches. Macro-level productivity effects are projected to remain modest over a decade, which tempers expectations of rapid, system-wide substitution even if model capability keeps climbing. The course's discussion-based, interpretive core and its GT-Pathways institutional anchor both act as independent brakes on displacement regardless of underlying AI competence. Given real uncertainty about both diffusion speed and how well AI calibration on contested political questions improves, a confident forecast of high displacement is unwarranted, but the direction of travel is toward greater rather than lesser exposure.
HON 1023.d: This course examines political societies and explores the basic ideas, structures, and issues of modern political systems in a comparative context.

r: World History since 1500 surveys social, cultural, religious, economic, and political themes across five centuries, work that is heavily content-synthesis and narrative-construction based rather than skills-practice based. Current models already summarize historical periods, compare causal narratives, and draft thematic essays competently, matching observed-usage data showing writing and research-synthesis tasks are among the most common consumer and enterprise AI uses today. The Honors seminar's discussion component adds interpretive debate over historiography and causation, but the underlying task, synthesizing established historical content, is less adversarial and lower-stakes than contested identity or ethics questions elsewhere in the Honors curriculum. That keeps AI competence for this course's core tasks meaningfully high today, even as the GT-HI1 designation and seminar format continue to slow how quickly that competence translates into reduced instrumental need.

By 2031, historical-content generation and comparative-thematic writing should be strongly AI-competent, consistent with capability-trend research projecting continued fast improvement on extended synthesis tasks, and productivity research on professional writing already shows large time savings with quality gains that plausibly transfer to historical essay drafting. Diffusion remains uneven, so classroom adoption likely lags what the technology could technically support. The seminar's live discussion of contested historiographical interpretation retains some protective value, but less than in courses built explicitly around adversarial critical reasoning. The GT-Pathways transfer-core mandate keeps the course institutionally anchored regardless of these capability trends. Overall, meaningful further displacement of instrumental need beyond the near-term level is plausible at this horizon, tempered mainly by adoption lag rather than by task difficulty.

Ten years out, if capability-trend projections around task-time-horizon doubling continue to hold, AI systems should competently handle most of the content-synthesis and comparative-narrative work this course currently teaches, including nuanced historiographical framing. Macro productivity estimates remain modest over a decade, which suggests actual classroom transformation could lag raw technical capability considerably. The Honors seminar's discussion format and the GT-Pathways institutional anchor persist as structural checks on displacement independent of AI competence, keeping some instrumental need intact even under optimistic capability assumptions. Given genuine uncertainty about diffusion pace and about how discussion-based history pedagogy adapts to ubiquitous AI drafting tools, continued upward pressure on displacement seems likely, but a confident point prediction beyond moderate-to-high exposure is not warranted by current evidence.
HON 1040.d: This course provides an introduction to important theories, concepts, methods and content for understanding world history since 1500. Among others, it explores social, cultural, religious, economic, and political themes.

r: General Biology I covers cellular and molecular biology, biochemical pathways, and genetics, explicitly serving as the foundation for every subsequent biology course in the sequence. Current models explain these concepts fluently and can tutor students through genetics or pathway problems, consistent with observed-usage data showing strong consumer use of AI for learning and explanation tasks. Because these are well-established, textbook-level scientific facts rather than contested or adversarial claims, verification burden for AI explanations is comparatively low, meaning less expert oversight is typically needed to catch errors. Even so, the course's explicit foundational-scaffolding role, building conceptual substrate that essentially all later biology coursework depends on, keeps instrumental need for actually taking the course intact regardless of how well AI can explain the same material to a student one-on-one.

By 2031, AI tutoring for foundational biology concepts should be highly capable and widely available, and capability-trend research on steadily improving task performance supports expecting continued gains in explanatory and problem-solving assistance for genetics and biochemical pathways specifically. Task-exposure research already associates well-defined, explainable science content with meaningful AI exposure, even though critical-thinking-heavy science work is separately flagged as more protected. The course's foundational-scaffolding role remains the dominant constraint: subsequent required biology coursework depends on this conceptual base regardless of whether AI can explain the same concepts effectively outside the structured course. That institutional dependency, not AI capability, is what continues to cap displacement of instrumental need at this horizon, even as AI's tutoring competence for the content itself keeps improving.

A ten-year horizon brings real uncertainty about whether personalized AI tutoring could substitute for structured foundational coursework entirely, especially if capability keeps compounding at rates implied by current task-horizon-doubling trends and adoption spreads into curricular design itself. That is a plausible trajectory, not a settled one: foundational science content built for a hard, verifiable domain (biology fundamentals) is exactly where AI explanation is currently strongest, per the low verification burden noted here. Yet the course's role as prerequisite substrate for essentially the entire biology curriculum is a structural, not merely a content-delivery, function, and that scaffolding role does not obviously dissolve just because explanatory competence improves. Continued moderate rather than high displacement seems most defensible, anchored by the foundational role rather than by any expectation AI cannot explain the material.
HON 1080.d: This introductory course serves as the foundation for all other biology courses. Emphasis is placed on cellular and molecular biology, biochemical pathways, and genetics.

r: General Biology Laboratory I introduces hands-on laboratory technique and the scientific method through mandatory, in-person wet-lab practice paired with HON 1080. This is fundamentally embodied, psychomotor work: pipetting, microscopy, specimen handling, and safety protocol, none of which current AI systems perform on a student's behalf, and task-exposure research consistently treats manual, physical work as low-exposure relative to text-based tasks. Verification burden is also high in the safety sense: a human must directly observe correct technique to prevent hazard, which is a fundamentally different check than verifying AI-generated text. The lab additionally functions as foundational scaffolding, introducing skills that subsequent lab-based science coursework depends on. Combined, these factors keep instrumental need for physically attending and performing this laboratory essentially undiminished at this horizon.

By 2031, AI-guided lab instruction and simulation tools should improve, and capability-trend research suggests continued fast progress in multimodal systems that could assist with protocol guidance or data-analysis support during lab sessions. But the physically embodied core, actually manipulating specimens and instruments, remains outside what deployed AI performs instead of the student, and diffusion data suggests real-world adoption of anything resembling robotic lab assistance in undergraduate teaching settings will lag laboratory-scale capability considerably. The safety-driven verification burden, requiring direct human observation of technique, persists independent of software capability gains. The course's foundational role for later lab-based coursework also continues unchanged. Instrumental need for hands-on attendance should remain largely intact, with AI functioning at most as a supplementary aid rather than a substitute for physical practice.

Ten years out, genuine uncertainty exists about how far lab-adjacent robotics and simulation could advance, and capability-trend research on rapid improvement leaves open a future where sophisticated virtual or robot-assisted lab experiences become far more capable than today's tools. Still, undergraduate laboratory pedagogy exists partly to build hands-on competence and safety judgment in the human directly, not merely to produce lab-report deliverables, and that embodied, safety-critical verification requirement is not obviously satisfied by remote or simulated alternatives even if they improve substantially. The course's foundational-scaffolding role for later lab-based science coursework further anchors instrumental need independent of tooling changes. A confident prediction of significant displacement is not warranted; embodiment and safety-verification protections identified in the evidence base appear durable across this horizon.
HON 1090.d: This mandatory laboratory accompanies HON 1080. This course introduces biology laboratory techniques, specifically exploring the scientific method.

r: HON 1311 introduces students to anthropology's core work: fieldwork methods, participant-observation, and cross-cultural interpretation of subsistence strategies, kinship, religion, and power relations tied to colonialism and inequality. These tasks map to Getting Information and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others, activities requiring situated, embodied engagement with informants that current models cannot replicate. Task-exposure research classifies science and critical-thinking-heavy interpretive work as negatively associated with AI exposure, while diffusion data (Census BTOS) shows only a minority of firms, let alone teaching programs, have operationalized AI for this kind of qualitative fieldwork training. The general-studies designation (Social and Behavioral Sciences, Global Diversity) makes this a required gtPathways transfer credit, an institutional mandate independent of automation potential. At 24 months, AI competently drafts background summaries but cannot perform the participant-observation exercises central to the course, keeping instrumental need low.

By five years, generative models will likely handle more of the course's literature synthesis and comparative-culture writing tasks—summarizing subsistence systems, kinship charts, and colonial-history readings—reflecting the steady rise the METR/Epoch trend describes in model task-time horizons. Observed-usage data already shows Computer & Mathematical and writing-adjacent tasks dominating consumer AI use, suggesting students will lean on AI for drafting essays about cultural relativism. Yet the course's fieldwork and participant-observation components remain interpersonal and situational, resisting full automation, and the general-studies designation (Social and Behavioral Sciences, Global Diversity) continues to function as a gtPathways transfer mandate that keeps enrollment demand structurally tied to the course regardless of task automation. This institutional lock caps the plausible rating at Medium rather than High even if writing tasks become largely AI-assisted, since the credit requirement itself does not automate away.

Ten years out, capability trends (METR/Epoch's doubling task-time horizon) make it plausible that AI could competently draft most cultural-comparison content and background research a student currently produces, though participant-observation fieldwork and situated ethnographic judgment remain far harder to specify or verify than desk research, and any projection this far carries real uncertainty. Even under an optimistic capability trajectory, the general-studies designation (Social and Behavioral Sciences, Global Diversity) preserves this course's gtPathways transfer-core status, an institutional requirement that does not dissolve with model capability and mechanically holds the rating at Medium rather than High. Macro estimates of AI's aggregate productivity effect over a decade remain modest, reinforcing that adoption inside teaching programs may still lag capability by 2036. The course's instrumental necessity is therefore capped by institutional mandate rather than by any confident claim about what fieldwork-based anthropology instruction will look like a decade from now.
HON 1311.d: Students explore the diversity that defines human experience. Students learn about the field of anthropology and its approach to examining other cultures with a focus on holism and cultural relativism. Students are introduced to fieldwork methods in anthropology and the importance of participant-observation in cultural anthropology. Students also examine various aspects of cultures across the globe, such as subsistence strategies, political organization, social identities and hierarchies, marriage, family and kinship systems, religious behavior, health, language, creative and artistic expressions, and issues of power in relation to colonialism, socio-economic discrimination, and global inequalities.

r: HON 1501 surveys contemporary health topics across biological, psychological, sociological, and cultural determinants, then asks students to plan and adopt healthier personal behaviors through experiential assignments. These tasks map to Getting Information, Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others, and Coaching and Developing Others—the last of which involves accountability and behavior-change work that current AI cannot enact on a student's behalf. Observed-usage data shows consumer AI concentrated in writing and information-lookup tasks, which suits the course's literature summaries but not its experiential behavior-change component. Task-exposure research still finds meaningful automation potential for health-information synthesis, yet actual classroom adoption lags that potential, per diffusion data showing only a minority of organizations operationalizing AI broadly. The general-studies designation (Social and Behavioral Sciences) fixes this course inside the gtPathways transfer core, an enrollment driver independent of how automatable its content becomes, keeping the 24-month instrumental-need rating low.

Within five years, AI health-information tools will likely draft more of the background material on biological, psychological, and sociological determinants that this course currently assigns as reading and writing tasks, consistent with observed automation-versus-augmentation patterns in the Anthropic Economic Index where enterprise use skews heavily toward automating information tasks. Productivity research on AI-assisted writing suggests students could produce polished health-behavior essays faster with AI drafting support. But the course's experiential requirement—planning and adopting a personal healthier behavior—resists substitution because it depends on individual accountability and lived follow-through, not information retrieval. The general-studies designation (Social and Behavioral Sciences) keeps HON 1501 inside the gtPathways transfer core regardless of these shifts, an institutional requirement that caps the rating at Medium; the course remains something students must complete for degree progress even as its informational content becomes easier to automate. This projection assumes continued but uneven diffusion of health-education AI tools.

By ten years, it is plausible that AI systems handle most of the informational and even coaching-style aspects of health-behavior planning this course teaches, given the capability trajectory METR and Epoch describe, though real behavior-change accountability and in-person experiential components remain difficult to fully delegate to a model, and any ten-year forecast for classroom practice carries substantial uncertainty. Macro productivity estimates suggest AI's aggregate economic effect over a decade stays modest, implying health-education programs may adopt automation unevenly even as underlying model capability advances further. Regardless of how far automation reaches into the course's content, the general-studies designation (Social and Behavioral Sciences) locks HON 1501 into the gtPathways transfer core, an institutional requirement unrelated to task automation that mechanically caps the rating at Medium rather than High. The course's instrumental value to a degree plan persists independent of whatever AI can do with health information by 2036.
HON 1501.d: This course investigates contemporary health topics. Subjects surveyed include current biological, psychological, sociological, and cultural factors that influence health. Experiential learning encourages students to plan and adopt healthier behaviors.

r: HON 2040 covers digestion, absorption, metabolism, and nutrient function as they relate to health and disease, declarative science content close to consumer health-information tasks like patient education handouts, meal-planning explainers, and basic dietary counseling scripts. Observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical and writing/office tasks dominate current deployment, and general nutrition explanation is well within today's chatbot competence for surface-level facts. Still, this is a GT-Pathways-designated (GT-SC2) natural-science course, meaning the state transfer-core mandate requires students complete a course in this category rather than letting AI substitute for it institutionally. Verification burden is moderate: nutrition misinformation carries real health consequences, so instructor-graded assessment of a student's grasp of metabolic pathways remains distinct from a chatbot summary. At 24 months, actual classroom adoption for credit-bearing instruction is limited, keeping instrumental need low despite the content's surface automatability.

By 2031, AI tutoring systems will likely handle much of the declarative explanation this course covers, since digestion pathways, macro- and micronutrient metabolism, and nutrient-disease relationships are stable, well-documented science with low ambiguity, matching the productivity-RCT pattern where novices see the largest gains from AI assistance on structured explanatory tasks. Task-exposure research associates programming and writing-adjacent explanatory work with higher exposure, and static nutrition content leans that direction more than open-ended scientific inquiry. The GT-SC2 designation still binds enrollment: the statutory 31-credit gen-ed transfer core requires a natural-science course from this pool, so institutional demand persists even as AI reduces the instrumental need to master content firsthand. Diffusion data suggests adoption across institutions remains uneven, meaning classroom practice lags capability. Confidence is moderate given the course's straightforward, content-transmission character rather than applied clinical judgment.

Ten years out, capability trends including task-time-horizon doubling every several months suggest AI systems will reliably explain and quiz students on nutrition science fundamentals, and could plausibly generate personalized study materials that substitute for much of the content-delivery function of a lecture-based course like this one. However, the GT-Pathways mandate is a state statutory requirement, not an institutional preference, so MSU Denver will still need to offer a qualifying natural-science option in this category regardless of how capable AI becomes at explaining metabolism. Macro-level productivity effects from AI remain modest over a decade per current estimates, and uneven diffusion across higher education could slow actual curricular substitution even where technically feasible. This horizon is genuinely uncertain; I would not commit to a confident prediction beyond noting content-delivery courses like this face more pressure than applied or clinical nutrition coursework.
HON 2040.d: This course is designed to provide students with an understanding of the fundamental concepts of human nutrition, including digestion, absorption, metabolism, and the function of nutrients as they relate to human health and disease.

r: HON 2110 asks students to compare personal theories of learning against scholarly research, collect evidence, and self-assess their own learning strategies, a metacognitive, self-referential task that AI cannot perform on a student's behalf, since the object of study is the student's own cognition. AI can summarize learning-science literature, a writing-adjacent task the Anthropic Economic Index shows is heavily used today, but the applied self-assessment and personal-practice components resist substitution because they require lived, first-person data the model does not possess. Verification burden is moderate rather than low: comparing personal theory to research literature is interpretive but not high-stakes or adversarial. The course carries only an institutional Social and Behavioral Sciences gen-ed designation, not a GT-Pathways code, so the credit-bearing requirement is real but softer than a statutory mandate. At 24 months, instrumental need remains low.

By 2031, AI assistants will likely be well-integrated into how students research learning theories and draft self-assessment reflections, and productivity research on professional writing tasks, showing faster completion and higher rated quality, suggests the literature-synthesis portion of this course becomes easier to offload. That said, task-exposure research finds critical-thinking-adjacent skills negatively associated with automation exposure, and this course's core deliverable, applying theory to one's own idiosyncratic learning practice, sits closer to that protected category than to routine writing. The gen-ed designation continues to generate enrollment demand independent of AI capability, though without a GT code the requirement is contributory rather than a hard statewide mandate, so substitution pressure could mount somewhat faster here than in GT-coded courses. I hold this at Medium with real uncertainty about how quickly self-assessment pedagogy gets automated in practice.

A decade out, personalized AI learning coaches could plausibly perform much of what this course teaches students to do for themselves, diagnosing a learner's strategies against research-based models and recommending adjustments, a capability adjacent to today's tutoring systems and consistent with the fast capability-doubling trend observed in recent estimates. Yet the course's stated purpose is developing the student's own metacognitive capacity, not producing a learning-strategy report, and that distinction is hard to fully automate away even as tools mature. Diffusion of AI into general-education curriculum design remains slow and uneven per current adoption data, and gen-ed requirement structures are sticky institutionally. I hedge significantly at this horizon: this could either remain a genuinely protected human-development course or be substantially reframed around AI-assisted metacognition, and the current description does not resolve which outcome is more likely.
HON 2110.d: In this course, students explore current theories, research, and applied practices regarding how people learn. Students analyze the assumptions underlying personal theories of learning in comparison to scholarly theory and research studies, collect evidence to support and challenge their views, and develop new ways of thinking about the learning process. Through the analysis of research- based strategies and emerging ideas about learning from social and behavioral sciences and other disciplines, students self-assess their own learning strategies and apply learning theories to their own practice.

r: HON 2750 is an interdisciplinary discussion seminar tracing contested definitions of selfhood across literary, philosophical, social-scientific, and artistic works from antiquity to the present, explicitly including debates about posthuman technology. This is critical-reasoning and interpretive-discussion work rather than fact retrieval: students construct and defend readings of primary texts in live seminar exchange. Task-exposure research finds science-and-critical-thinking skills negatively associated with AI exposure, and open-ended interpretive discussion of contested humanistic claims sits squarely in that protected zone; verification burden is high because judging the quality of a novel interpretive argument requires the same expertise being taught, not a checkable fact. The jagged-frontier finding that AI users perform worse outside the model's competence, with miscalibrated trust, reinforces why an instructor's live evaluation of argumentation cannot currently be replaced. At 24 months, instrumental need is low.

AI language tools by 2031 will readily generate plausible-sounding essays synthesizing theories of the self across disciplines, and observed-usage data confirms writing tasks are already heavily used today. But the seminar's actual work, real-time discussion, defending interpretations against pushback, and building thematic connections collaboratively, is not reducible to a written product, and verification burden stays high because assessing the soundness of a contested humanistic claim needs the same disciplinary judgment an instructor is cultivating in students. The course carries only an institutional Arts and Humanities gen-ed designation, not a GT code, so its enrollment driver is real but not statutorily locked. I expect continued but still-limited encroachment: AI becomes a research aid for background material while the seminar's discursive core remains distinctly human-mediated at this horizon.

Ten years is long enough that capability could shift substantially, given task-time-horizon doubling trends, but interpretive humanities discussion built on live argumentation and verification-heavy claims about contested cultural material is among the categories task-exposure research most consistently protects. I would not predict confidently that seminar-based instruction in this mode disappears; the binding constraint is that judging a novel interpretation of the self across cultures requires exactly the expertise the course builds, which is not a checkable, low-verification-burden task even for a highly capable model. Diffusion remains slow and uneven per current adoption figures, and macro productivity effects from AI stay modest over a decade in current estimates. Genuine uncertainty remains about how discussion pedagogy evolves alongside AI tools, but the instrumental case for eliminating this course looks weak even at this horizon.
HON 2750.d: In this interdisciplinary course, students learn about how grand narratives have shaped and transformed notions of subjectivity over time, from the ancient and/or medieval world through the present day. The focus is on works that have had a literary, philosophical, social scientific, and artistic impact on the notion of the self. Students consider contested definitions for "the self" over time and in different cultures. HON 2770.d: This course is an interdisciplinary inquiry where students learn about the dynamics of social change. Discussions focus on important examples of radical social transformation throughout history and from around the globe. The jagged-frontier finding that AI users are notably less accurate when working outside a model's core competence, often without recognizing it, is particularly relevant to historical-scientific interpretation, where confident-sounding but wrong syntheses are a known risk. Diffusion of AI into humanities-inflected science-studies instruction remains slow and uneven per current adoption data. HON 2800.d: In this course students learn about the initial discoveries that sparked new scientific fields and about the subsequent revolutions caused by such discoveries. By examining the role of the scientific method in the production of knowledge, students improve their own scientific literacy and learn to critically examine historical scientific experiments. HON 2850.d: Technology's impact on human life emerges in a wide array of fields such as agriculture, medicine, warfare, politics, education, transportation, space exploration, communication, data science and robotics. In this interdisciplinary course, students consider definitions of technology and examine the historical relationship between humans and technology. Task-exposure research finds that science- and critical-thinking-heavy cognitive work is negatively associated with AI exposure even as writing tasks generally are positively associated, and multidisciplinary theoretical synthesis of this kind sits closer to the critical-thinking pole. That gap between fluent surface synthesis and defensible theoretical argument, layered onto critical-thinking-heavy work's documented negative association with exposure, keeps realized automatability low even as drafting assistance grows. The general-studies designation (Arts and Humanities) independently locks this course into the gtPathways transfer core, but does not by itself push the rating past what the underlying task content supports at this horizon.

Over ten years, it is plausible that models further close the gap on multidisciplinary theoretical synthesis, given the pace of capability growth METR and Epoch document, and realized task automation likely rises correspondingly—but any confident forecast about AI's ability to produce rigorous, textually grounded critical-theory argumentation across ten overlapping schools of thought by 2036 is unwarranted given today's evidence. Task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking-heavy cognitive work is negatively associated with exposure may weaken as capability advances, yet Acemoglu-style macro estimates put AI's economy-wide productivity effect at a modest ceiling over a decade, suggesting slow, uneven translation of raw capability into classroom practice. Independent of that trajectory, the general-studies designation (Arts and Humanities) locks HON 2950 into the gtPathways transfer core, an institutional requirement that caps the rating at Medium regardless of how automatable the interpretive work eventually becomes. This is a hedged, capped Medium rather than a confident High.
HON 2950.d: In the Modern Period, Critical Theory emerges as a decidedly multidisciplinary field that challenges the foundations of the existing social order through in-depth analysis of capitalism, culture, power, the family, and the individual. Students conduct an overview of the development of the field of Critical Theory and examines some of its major currents. Topics may include: Psychoanalytic Criticism, Marxist Criticism, Discourse Theory, Feminist Criticism/Gender Studies/Queer Theory, Deconstruction, Race Theory, Postmodernism, New Historicism, Cultural Studies, Narratology, and Digital Media Studies.

HON 3101.d: This course is designed to provide in-depth sociological, historical and political analyses of community-based organizations, the process by which they originated, leadership styles, and information relative to their missions and functions within the Chicana/o community. I hedge considerably at this horizon: capability trends suggest fast improvement is plausible, but macro adoption remains slow and uneven under current diffusion data, and a non-expert instructor or student still cannot easily verify whether an AI-generated spectroscopic interpretation is correct, which sustains real verification burden even as raw capability rises. HON 3190.d: This course provides a one-semester survey of the principles of thermodynamics, equilibrium, kinetics, quantum mechanics, and spectroscopy.

HON 3460.d: This course will provide students with a general background on Chicana feminist thought. Chicana feminism has carved out a discursive space for Chicanas and other women of color, a space where they can articulate their experiences at the intersection of race, class, gender, and sexuality, among other considerations. In the process, Chicana feminists have critically challenged Chicano nationalist discourse as well as European and North American feminism. The course will address the diversity in thinking and methodology that defines these discourses thus acknowledging the existence of a variety of feminisms that occur within Chicana intellectual thought. The course will also explore the diversity of realms in which this feminist thinking is applied: labor, education, cultural production (literature, art, performance, etc.), sexuality, and spirituality, among others.

A decade out, AI will be a highly capable interlocutor able to generate and even role-play opposing viewpoints on demand, and the balance of this variable-topics course could plausibly shift toward AI-assisted debate preparation or structured critique of machine-generated positions. Capability trends point toward steadily lengthening task-time horizons, so the technical ceiling for producing synthesis prose will be far above today's. Still, the central pedagogical transaction, a student building and defending an interdisciplinary argument live among peers, is not a task an AI performs for the student; it is a competence the student must personally exercise. Given the honest uncertainty about how seminar pedagogy adapts under ubiquitous AI drafting tools, and the continued protection from real-time interpersonal exchange, the rating holds Low, with the caveat that this is the softest of the three horizons.
HON 3910.d: This variable topics course provides students with the opportunity to examine historical and/or contemporary issues from interdisciplinary perspectives. Course activities include relevant readings from a variety of perspectives and disciplines, discussions encouraging synthesis and analysis of conflicting or competing views, and written assignments.

HON 4670.d: This course enriches students' understanding of a variety of theoretical models that have influenced contemporary critical practice in cinema studies. Students explore examples of theory and criticism from a range of periods and approaches, with a primary focus on key theories that have emerged in the last forty years. r: This one-credit seminar prepares Honors students to write a thesis: developing a thesis statement, project outline, initial bibliography, and working abstract, and identifying a faculty Thesis Advisor. Yet the requirement that a qualified Thesis Advisor evaluate and approve the resulting proposal before the student proceeds to the Senior Honors Thesis is a structural feature of the Honors curriculum, not an artifact of current AI capability, and verification of originality and feasibility remains a human judgment call. Given real uncertainty about how proposal-stage advising evolves under mature AI tools, the honest read is that the drafting labor keeps automating while the advisor-verification core persists. The rating holds Medium, not lower, reflecting genuine but partial erosion.
HON 4948.d: This course is taken prior to the Senior Honors Thesis (HON 4950) and is only open to Honors students. This course familiarizes students with project organization and the scope and proper format of an undergraduate thesis project. Each student develops: a thesis statement, a project outline, an initial bibliography and a working abstract. Students also identify a primary Thesis Advisor for their projects. The Thesis Advisor is a faculty member with expertise in a discipline closely related to the topic of the thesis project.

A decade out, AI research tools will plausibly handle substantial portions of literature synthesis, data processing, and even prose drafting across disciplines, and macro-level diffusion estimates suggest measurable but modest aggregate productivity effects from such tools rather than wholesale task replacement. The severe verification burden on certifying that scholarly or creative work is genuinely the student's own reasoning, combined with the embodied, real-time nature of the oral defense, keeps a knowledgeable human necessary in the loop regardless of how capable AI drafting assistance becomes. HON 4950.d: The Honors Thesis is the culmination of the Honors undergraduate experience. The Thesis Advisor is a faculty member with expertise in a discipline closely related to the topic of the thesis project. Students submit a written thesis and deliver a public oral presentation of their work.

The genuine uncertainty is how heavily AI tools are woven into the research and drafting process by 2036, not whether the verification-and-defense structure persists; that structure is a feature of the Honors curriculum's design rather than a function of current AI limitations. Embodiment of the oral presentation and the severe verification burden on original scholarship both continue to cap the rating. It holds Low, the most confidently protected course in this batch.
HON 4951.d: The Paired Honors Thesis is the culmination of the Honors undergraduate experience. This one-credit course must be paired with an upper division departmental Senior Experience, research or capstone course. In this course, students complete an independent research and/or creative project under the direction of a primary Thesis Advisor and the Honors Director. The Thesis Advisor is a faculty member with expertise in a discipline closely related to the topic of the thesis project. Students submit a written thesis and deliver a public oral presentation of their work.
